- The failure is triggered in `ResettingEvent.g(t, y)` because `g` is called with `t = 7.796...` after an event at `10.99` has already been triggered, so time goes backwards.
- The deepest project method in the trace is `EventState.evaluateStep`, but its logic uses `interpolator.getPreviousTime()` / `getCurrentTime()`, which are the interpolator’s soft times. Statistically, that part looks consistent.
- The stronger evidence points one frame up, in `AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep(...)`, where the integrator splits one accepted step around an event and then reuses the same interpolator for the “remaining part” of the step:
  - it first restricts the interpolator to `[previousT, eventT]`
  - handles the event
  - then resets the interpolator to `[eventT, currentT]`
  - then immediately calls `currentEvent.evaluateStep(interpolator)` again
- This reuse is the dangerous operation. The test’s assertion explicitly says the bug is that `g` is called at obsolete times after a later event was already triggered. That is exactly the kind of symptom caused by `acceptStep` orchestrating reevaluation on an interpolator segment that is not fully consistent after event/reset handling.
- `EventState.evaluateStep(...)` itself computes substep times from its local start/end interval and does not obviously manufacture an earlier time on its own. The bad chronology is more plausibly introduced by the caller’s step-splitting/reuse protocol in `acceptStep(...)`.

So the root cause is most likely that `acceptStep(...)` incorrectly re-evaluates events on the remaining part of a step after an event/reset, leading to stale/interleaved interpolator state and backward-time calls to `g`.

The most suspicious buggy method is:

`org.apache.commons.math.ode.AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep(org.apache.commons.math.ode.sampling.AbstractStepInterpolator,double[],double[],double)`

Diagnosis:
- The failure is triggered in `ResettingEvent.g(t, y)` because `g` is called with `t = 7.796...` after an event at `10.99` has already been triggered, so time goes backwards.
- The deepest project method in the trace is `EventState.evaluateStep`, but its logic uses `interpolator.getPreviousTime()` / `getCurrentTime()`, which are the interpolator’s soft times. Statistically, that part looks consistent.
- The stronger evidence points one frame up, in `AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep(...)`, where the integrator splits one accepted step around an event and then reuses the same interpolator for the “remaining part” of the step:
  - it first restricts the interpolator to `[previousT, eventT]`
  - handles the event
  - then resets the interpolator to `[eventT, currentT]`
  - then immediately calls `currentEvent.evaluateStep(interpolator)` again
- This reuse is the dangerous operation. The test’s assertion explicitly says the bug is that `g` is called at obsolete times after a later event was already triggered. That is exactly the kind of symptom caused by `acceptStep` orchestrating reevaluation on an interpolator segment that is not fully consistent after event/reset handling.
- `EventState.evaluateStep(...)` itself computes substep times from its local start/end interval and does not obviously manufacture an earlier time on its own. The bad chronology is more plausibly introduced by the caller’s step-splitting/reuse protocol in `acceptStep(...)`.

So the root cause is most likely that `acceptStep(...)` incorrectly re-evaluates events on the remaining part of a step after an event/reset, leading to stale/interleaved interpolator state and backward-time calls to `g`.
